history.player:
My character: Rowan Garvey. A twenty-three-year-old human man with brown skin, unruly dark hair, and ink-stained fingers, wearing a carefully mended charcoal coat and the inherited Garvey signet. Newly arrived and unsure of Conclave customs. He grew up unaware of his heritage, lost his parents young, and does not know whether he has any magic.

Begin the story shortly before the welcome dinner, in my room at Garvey House. I play Rowan Garvey.
history.story:
The last of the daylight lies in a long bar across a bed made too neatly to have been slept in. A trunk stamped with a law office's seal waits beneath the window; the clothes sent ahead have been hung in the wardrobe with exacting care. Your mended charcoal coat rests over the back of a chair, and the Garvey signet catches a muted glint in the fading light.

On the desk, beside the Academy primer, a narrow brass frame holds a sheet of browned paper. The salutation reads *My dear Willan,* in a firm, slanted hand. The rest is an ordinary request about a delayed visit, a basket of pears, and whether he will remember to bring the blue folio his aunt left in the city. It closes with an irritated postscript about rain.

From below comes the softened clatter of plates and the brief scrape of a chair across the dining hall floor. A laugh rises, then breaks into several voices too blurred by the stairwell to separate. The house has begun doing something without you.

Three measured knocks sound at the door. A warm gold wash of light gathers beneath the threshold, thin as spilled candlelight.

“Rowan Garvey?

The lamps are lit below.
I am Seraphel Dawnquill.

Rashid has counted the chairs twice.
I think a third count
will make him declare the table a border.

May I show you the way?”

history.player: I pull on my coat and open the door. “Please. I'd hate to cause an international incident before dinner.” I smile, then glance back at the framed letter. “Do you know who Willan was? Someone's put his letter beside my bed, and I'm trying to work out how much of this house has anything to do with my family.”
history.story:
The door opens onto the second-floor landing and a young woman in white and gold. Her honey-blonde hair is pinned back from her face; the small wings at her shoulders lie close enough that their tips nearly brush the doorframe. Her warmth is mostly light, a soft glow along the hall's dark wood.

“Then we will postpone it
until after the soup.
A ruined meal is harder to forgive.

I do not know Willan.
The frame was there last term
when I was shown the rooms.
Professor Stone may know.
He keeps old names in his head
and sometimes resents lending them out.”

She turns toward the stairs without waiting to make the uncertainty larger than it is. The landing opens onto the common room below: portraits in heavy frames watching over the oversized fireplace, leather chairs pushed back from study tables, a pair of discarded books facedown near the grate. Beyond its wide arch, the dining hall is all candlelight and polished wood. A server in blue Academy livery passes through with a covered dish, and the smell of roasted citrus and pepper follows him.

The long table has places set for seventeen. At its middle, Rashid is moving a cluster of name cards by fractions of an inch. Fine dark fur shows along the back of one hand beneath an immaculate cuff. He looks up as Seraphel brings you through the doorway; his attention takes in the coat, the signet, and the fact of you with the same quick efficiency.

“Good,” he says. “We have avoided a diplomatic disaster before the first course.” He lifts one of the cards, where *GARVEY* has been written in a formal black hand. “The staff asked whether to use your house name or your given one. I told them I would rather ask than invent a custom for you. Rowan, Garvey, or something else?”

history.player: “Rowan, please. If everyone says Garvey, I'll keep thinking they mean the building.” I offer Rashid my hand. “And thank you for asking.” I lower my voice a little. “Seraphel mentioned Professor Stone. I'd like to speak to him about a family letter, if there's a chance after dinner.” Then I take my place at the table. The smell of the food has reminded me how long ago lunch was.
history.story:
Rashid takes your hand in a firm, brief clasp. “Rowan, then.” His voice drops with yours. “Stone is usually in the library after dinner. He may know about the letter. He may also decide the answer is less urgent than whatever he is reading, but that is a risk you can take with your own time.”

He puts the Garvey card down, draws a line through the surname with the tip of his pen, and writes *ROWAN* beneath it in smaller letters. When you take the chair, Seraphel settles to your left, folding her wings with practiced care. Across the table, a tall woman with black-red horns swept back from severely tied hair watches Rashid return the pen to his pocket.

“You will give him names before petitions,” she says.

Rashid's mouth shifts. “A fair correction.”

The woman inclines her head toward you. “Ashara vel Kothren. Welcome, Rowan.” There is a trace of heat in the air when she reaches for her water glass. “Rashid believes orderly introductions are an affront to efficiency.”

“I believe they can survive until the first course,” Rashid says. A server sets a platter between two candles: sliced pheasant glazed with bitter orange, potatoes crisped in their skins, a dark green sauce fragrant with pepper and herbs. The first proper scent of food reaches the table whole.

Rashid pulls a folded sheet from beside his place setting but leaves it closed under one hand. “There is one thing I will ask when you have had a chance to eat. The Academy closed the covered court after an injury, including the supervised evening sessions some of us use. I am collecting signatures for a request to reopen it with oversight.” He looks directly at you. “After dinner, would you read it and decide whether you want your name on it?”

history.player: “I'll read it,” I tell Rashid, “though I don't know enough to promise a signature yet. What do people actually do in the covered court?” I serve myself some pheasant and potatoes, then smile at Ashara. “Thank you for the welcome. I'm rather relieved to have reached the eating part.” As dinner goes on, I listen to the conversation around me and enjoy having a hot meal without having to hurry through it.
history.story:
“That is all I asked,” Rashid says. “Mostly we drill: footwork, falls, partner work, basic wards. Some people use blunted blades. It is an evening practice group for students who are not on the Military track, not a militia pretending to be one.” His thumb stays on the folded petition. “The injured student was in a partner drill. I have accounts from the people who were there. I have not seen the instructor's report.”

“Then the request should say exactly what supervision you want,” Ashara says. “A supervised evening session is not the same as a private booking, and it should not pretend to be.”

Two seats farther down, the gold-haired man in white and gold sets down his wine. “Nor should it pretend that no one was hurt. A temporary closure is not an injustice merely because it inconveniences us.”

“No,” Rashid says, still even. “An indefinite one is.”

The server returns with a basket of bread before either can take the point farther. The pheasant is tender beneath its orange glaze; the potatoes crack open with salt and steam. For a few minutes the table is occupied by the uncomplicated work of eating.

Introductions come in pieces rather than ceremony. The man in white and gold gives a precise nod. “Aldric Verantus.” A pale, silver-haired woman beside him says, “Caelindra Vaeyn,” as if the name has already been placed in the proper order. Across from Seraphel, the white-haired woman who has been studying the candle flames offers, “Ysolde Thornmantle.” The small woman with blue-black hair and entirely black eyes lifts her glass last.

“Thessaly Morrow,” she says. “I have no title that improves it.”

“A useful policy,” Caelindra says, and reaches for the bread.

The table gradually finds a less formal rhythm. Aldric and Caelindra discover that they both object to the way first-years are required to sign for bridge access, though not for the same reasons. Thessaly declares the pear wine not worth its price, accepts a second glass when the server offers one, and adds that the second is included in dinner. Even Caelindra's mouth gives a brief, unwilling shift at that.

Ysolde says little until the conversation turns to the storm below the Academy. Then she explains why the western terrace makes its clouds look green at sunset, tracing the angle of the garden lamps with one cool fingertip on the tablecloth. She continues through the arrival of a dark berry tart, absorbed enough that the detail becomes a small account of wind, height, and the difficulty of seeing a bridge in heavy rain. Seraphel listens with her chin propped on one hand and answers, when Ysolde finally stops:

“On the third stair
the storm hid every door.
I followed the smell of tea
and found the chapel pantry.”

Rashid laughs first; Ashara follows a moment later.

By the time the final cups are cleared, the petition is still folded beside Rashid's place. He does not raise it again. Beyond the dining hall, the common room has gone quieter around its fire. At the far end, the library door stands open a hand's breadth. A single lamp burns somewhere past its threshold, and the air carries the dry, familiar smell of oil and old paper.

history.player: I thank the others for dinner, then tell Rashid, “I'm going to try the library while the professor's still up. I'll find you about the petition afterward.” I go upstairs to fetch the letter in its brass frame. At the library door, I knock lightly. “Professor Stone? I'm Rowan Garvey. Seraphel thought you might recognise this.” I hold the frame by its edges. “My parents died when I was small. I haven't much family history to bring with me, and I'd like to know who Willan was.”
history.story:
Rashid folds the petition into his inner pocket at your words. “All right. I will be in the common room for a while.” Ashara gives you a short nod over the remains of her tart. Seraphel's parting wish follows you to the doorway.

“May the shelves be kind.
May the answers be smaller
than the questions.”

By the time you return from the second floor with the brass frame, the dining hall has begun to empty around the last cups. The library door is still ajar. Inside, lamplight pools over a broad desk and climbs the iron spiral stair in thin bands. A man with greying hair sits amid several open volumes, his coat hung over the back of his chair. At your knock, he looks up, then rises and opens the door fully.

“I know,” he says. His eyes settle on the frame before they return to you. “Rowan Garvey.”

He does not take it from you. Instead he bends close enough to read the page through the glass. For a moment, the only sound is the soft tick of a cooling lamp.

“Lenora Garvey,” he says at last. “I recognize the hand before I recognize Willan. She wrote to half the family as though each of them had misplaced something important.” One corner of his mouth moves, then stills. “Willan was one of her great-nephews, from another Garvey branch. He was expected to visit. He did not. This letter will not tell us why, and I would rather not invent a tragedy because an aunt mentioned pears.”

Stone straightens and glances toward the orderly shelves behind him. “I keep an index of the old human household papers. It may give you his parents and a later address, if anything was recorded. I cannot tell from memory whether his line meets yours.” He looks back at the brass frame. “Would you leave it with me overnight so I can check?”

history.player: “Yes. Thank you.” I set the frame carefully on a clear part of the desk. “I'd like to come back tomorrow.” I turn the signet around my finger. “Is Lenora connected to the inheritance that brought me here? I think I saw a family name by the bed and hoped it would turn out to be someone close.” I look at the letter again. “Though being the sort of aunt who sends pears isn't a bad thing to learn about someone.”
history.story:
Stone waits until the frame is safely on the desk before he answers. His attention catches briefly on the signet as it turns, then returns to the letter.

“Yes. Lenora is connected to the inheritance.” He pulls a small, leather-bound notebook from beneath one of the open volumes but does not open it yet. “She was an aunt to your grandfather. The branch that led to you passed through her younger brother's children. She is not a direct ancestor, but she belongs to the same household line. The solicitors did not find you by chasing a name through unrelated families.”

He adjusts the frame until it sits square with the desk's edge. “Willan was kin through another branch. That is the ordinary answer, I am afraid. Families tend to look more dramatic from a distance than they do in their records.”

For the first time, his expression softens into something almost companionable. “The pears are useful information, though. They tell us Lenora was expecting someone she cared to feed, and that she had strong opinions about whether he would remember his papers.”

Stone taps the closed notebook once. “Tomorrow evening, after your first day has had its way with you, come back here. I will have the household index ready. It may not give you a grand revelation, but it should give you more than a framed letter and a missing visit.”

history.player: “That already gives me something to picture. Thank you, Professor. Tomorrow evening, then.” I leave him to his books and return to the common room to find Rashid. “I've come to read your page before the fire puts me to sleep.” I sit down near him and give the petition a proper read, particularly what it asks the Academy to change.
history.story:
The common room has settled into the softer part of evening. The fire has burned down to a red, steady bed beneath the portraits, and most of the study tables are empty. Rashid sits in one of the leather chairs with his jacket unbuttoned, a second sheet of paper balanced on the armrest beside him. At your words, he draws the petition from his pocket and hands it over.

“Read all of it,” he says. “I would rather have a refusal based on the words than a name added because I asked.”

The page is headed in a clear, compact hand:

*Petition for Limited Supervised Access to the Covered Court*

*We request that the current full closure be replaced, pending review, by two supervised evening practice periods each week. Those periods would use inspected equipment, follow the posted safety limits, and exclude ranked or unsupervised sparring.*

*We further request a short written account of the incident's relevant safety findings, without naming the injured student; a statement of what supervision the Academy considers necessary; and a date and criteria for reconsidering full access.*

*No signatory contends that the injury was trivial. We contend that a precaution meant to prevent another injury should not eliminate the only regular supervised practice available to students without private instruction or court time.*

Below that, the signatures begin with a handful of unfamiliar names and leave room for more. There is no account of the injury beyond what Rashid said at dinner, no guess at fault, and no attempt to make the injured student into an argument.

“I can ask them for access, a supervisor, and an explanation of the rule,” Rashid says when you have had the page a moment. “I cannot honestly claim I know why the accident happened. If the report says the court itself is unsafe, we will need a different request.” His eyes settle on the wording rather than on you. “What would you change before you put your name anywhere near it?”

history.player: “I don't think I'd change it. You're asking them to explain themselves and make room for people who can't buy their own lessons. I can support that.” I sign Rowan Garvey beneath the other names and return the page. “If you do get a session back, I'd like to try it. I can't promise anything with wards, but I expect I could learn to fall over.” I stay by the fire for a little while, then say goodnight and go to bed. In the morning, I consult the primer to work out where a new arrival is supposed to begin his day.
history.story:
Rashid reads the new signature once, then folds the petition with more care than he used at dinner. “Then I will make sure the first thing you learn is how to fall without bruising your pride. Wards can wait.” He tucks the paper away again. “If we get the sessions back, I will hold you to that.”

For a while, the fire gives the room enough occupation. Rashid tells you about the first balance drill he ever attempted: a low beam over a sand pit, an instructor who refused to accept that a well-made argument could improve his footing, and the precise moment he discovered she had been right. “She called it an educational compromise,” he says. “I was twelve and did not speak to her for three days.”

The house quiets around the fire. When you leave for the night, Rashid is still in the chair with a book open across one knee and the petition safely out of sight.

Morning light reaches the room pale and clean through the garden-facing window. The primer's first pages are less history than instruction. A stiff leaf of paper has been tucked into the binding under the heading *First Day for New Conclave Students.*

*Breakfast is available in the dining hall from first bell. At third bell, all first-year Conclave students are to report to the Conclave Seminar Room for orientation, course registration, and the Academy address. Bring this primer and your proof of admission. Do not report to a track seminar or faculty office before orientation unless specifically summoned.*

Below it, a small diagram marks the route from Garvey House through the quadrangle: past the gardens, beneath the low dragon-carved arch, then along the marble-and-black-stone walk to the oval-door entrance of the seminar room. The third bell has not yet sounded.

history.player: I check my belongings for the proof of admission, get dressed, and take the primer down to breakfast. Then I set off early, following the diagram rather carefully; I'd rather have time to get lost and recover. At orientation I choose a seat where I can hear and pay attention to the courses on offer. I'm especially interested in what someone can learn here if he doesn't yet know whether he has any magic.
history.story:
The proof of admission is in the lawyers' packet beneath a list of garments and household effects: a stiff cream card stamped with the Academy seal, naming Rowan Garvey as a first-year Conclave student. The Garvey signet is noted beside it as identification, not decoration.

Breakfast is quiet at this hour, the long dinner table reduced to a few places and a pot of strong tea. By the time you leave the house with the primer in hand, the gardens are bright with flowers that have no business blooming together. The diagram proves reliable. Pale paths carry you past clipped hedges and the low dragon-carved arch into the quadrangle, where black stone, white marble, and living timber meet under the slow flicker of the lamp-globes fading with the morning.

The seminar room's oval door is open when you arrive. Inside, the fifteen chairs circle a table in polished dark wood; the framed Accords around the walls repeat themselves in seven different scripts. There is time to choose a clear seat before the other first-years begin to file in, speaking in low fragments or not speaking at all.

At third bell, Chancellor Ashworth enters with a narrow stack of course sheets. Age has silvered his hair, but there is nothing fragile in the clean line of his white-and-gold robes. He waits until the last chair has stopped moving.

“The Conclave is not a reward for being finished,” he says. “It is preparation for work that will outlast the Academy. This term, every one of you will study Covenant Law, practical rhetoric, and comparative institutions. The rest of your programme is chosen for what you need to understand, not for what anyone expects you to become.”

He passes the sheets around the table. Beneath the required courses are smaller studios: Treaty Languages and Records; Political Economy; Land, Borders, and Supply; Conflict De-escalation; and *Magical Literacy and Safe Practice.* The last is marked open to any student, with a note in smaller type: *No casting required. Covers active workings, consent, wards, hazard recognition, and requesting qualified aid.*

Ashworth's finger rests briefly on that line as he continues. “No student is admitted on a promise of power. If you cannot cast a ward, you may still learn to read one, question its terms, and recognize when it is unsafe to proceed. If you are uncertain whether you can cast, the Arcana faculty offers private aptitude consultations after the first week. They are assessments, not verdicts.”

At the bottom of the page, a separate line names the afternoon's introduction to the Academy library and tomorrow's first meetings with Professors Windwhisper and Kira. The studio choices are due at the end of the week.
